description: We’re M.A.P.S., a four-person team that turns space science into playable missions. We bring together scientific research, storytelling, game design, and web development. If you enjoy making complex ideas fun to explore, we’d love to connect with people who bring skills in game art, sound design, or playtesting.
summary:
M.A.P.S. is a browser game where players run a fictional space agency and take on four missions. In Moon Mission, they choose a launcher, land near the lunar south pole, and try to bring back evidence of ice. In Ganymede, they equip a crewed expedition, manage radiation and power, and drill through an icy surface. In The Crimson Sky, they investigate why the sky turns red worldwide, analyze evidence, and design spacecraft to test their hypotheses. In ATALAYA, they build and operate a CubeSat to gather data that could help forecasters warn communities about hurricanes.

The game addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by linking launch, spacecraft, ground operations, and the people who use the data. Players make choices about instruments, payload, fuel, power, and communications, then see what those choices enable in flight and what the mission delivers. NASA resources such as LCROSS, LRO, and IceCube, along with ESA’s Juice mission, inform campaign design.

We built M.A.P.S. to help players understand why engineering teams make trade-offs. By flying a lander, testing evidence, or trying to deliver a useful observation during a crisis, players can see how a choice on the design table changes what a mission can achieve.
details:
What it does and how it works

M.A.P.S. brings four playable campaigns together in one browser game. Each gives players a different objective and carries their design choices through to flight, operations, and the final outcome.

  • Moon Mission: The Rocket’s Fine Print. Design a lunar south pole mission, select a launcher and payload, fly the descent, and investigate the surface. The final report shows which observations reached Earth and which samples made it back.
  • Ganymede: The Integrated Front. Equip a crewed expedition to Jupiter’s icy moon, choose a route, respond to a solar storm, allocate power for drilling, and decide what the crew can bring home. Fuel, cargo, and crew health affect the ending.
  • The Crimson Sky. Follow a protagonist from São Paulo as the sky turns red worldwide. Explore a 2.5D story world, examine evidence, design spacecraft, align signals, plan burns, and book ground station passes to test competing explanations.
  • ATALAYA. Select an instrument, build and test a hurricane-observation CubeSat, then operate it in orbit. The mission succeeds by getting useful observations to the people who need them in time.

Benefits and intended impact

Students and curious players can explore why mission teams make trade-offs. A heavier instrument might improve what the team can measure and force it to leave another component behind. Mission results show how those choices affected what the crew achieved. Where team play is available, players also practice sharing priorities and making decisions together.

Tools, languages, and hardware

We built the game with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We used Three.js and WebGL for 3D scenes, React in Ganymede, and Vite to build ATALAYA. The game uses browser audio and local storage. PeerJS and WebRTC support online rooms in compatible campaigns. We used GitHub for version control and GitHub Pages to host the public build. We developed the game for desktop computers with a WebGL-capable browser.

Creativity and design considerations

Each campaign makes a different part of space engineering playable. Players can brake a lunar lander, keep a crew safe during a solar storm, connect evidence to a hypothesis, or get a hurricane observation to a forecaster. We considered scientific accuracy, difficulty, teamwork, and the clarity of feedback. NASA and partner-agency resources ground the campaigns in real examples. Fictional scenarios and simplified calculations make the decisions manageable during play.
